content:
To inform Members of the financial performance of the
Council as at the end of July.  Members
are asked to approve any proposed changes to the capital
programme and revenue
budget.

Cabinet considered the report
of the Director of Finance which set out the financial performance
of the Council at the first review of the 2026-27 financial year,
covering the period from 1 April 2026 to 31 July 2026. It
summarised the key headlines for financial performance, covering
revenue and capital budgets.
 
Members noted Cheshire
West and Chester, along with Councils nationally, continued to face
significant financial pressure with the forecasted overspend of
£11.6 million reduced to £9.4 million at the end of
July 2026. This was following identified mitigating actions of
£2.2 million. Significant financial challenges continued
across most service areas but particularly within Adults and
Children’s Services, where demand-led pressures, high-cost
placements, home-to-school transport costs and delays in delivering
planned savings contributed to the overspend. The Dedicated Schools
Grant also faced a substantial forecast deficit due to rising SEND
demand and an increase in Education, Health and Care Plans
(EHCP’s). However, with recent national SEND Reform plans,
local authorities were eligible to apply for a ‘High Needs
Stability Grant’ from the Department of Education to support
the deficit. This is dependent on approval of the Council’s
SEND reform plan. There is also currently a statutory override
until 31 March 2028 so the deficit does not impact on general
reserve.
 
Members were advised
that all service areas had been directed to take immediate action
to ensure further mitigations to reduce forecast pressure. Failure
to implement these mitigations would impact the Councils’
financial resilience and would result in general reserves below the
Council’s assessed safe range if not addressed. Members were
informed that the capital programme remained largely on track
alongside proposed investment in community facilities and
infrastructure projects. Members were reassured that Council
management had a clear understanding of where the financial
pressures lay and had already initiated a range of actions to
reduce expenditure, accelerate savings delivery and strengthen the
Council’s financial resilience.
 
Councillor Carol Gahan, Cabinet Member for Finance and Legal,
led the discussion on the item as proposer and the item was
seconded by Councillor Louise Gittins, Leader of the
Council.
 
Visiting Members: Councillor Charles Hardy spoke in relation to
the item.
 
Cabinet welcomed the comprehensive report and recognised the
ongoing challenges and financial pressures in key areas. Members
noted that whilst overspend was significant, with the increase in
high cost social care placements and EHCP’s having seen even
more additional demand than previous years, efforts to reduce the
pressure remained robust whilst welfare services remained stable
and protected. Members also acknowledged that capital projects
remained a focus for the council which they felt further
highlighted the achievements of teams across the Council. Councill
staff were thanked for their hard work.
 
DECIDED:     That
 
Financial Performance:
 

1)           
the forecast revenue and capital outturn of the Council as set out
in this report be noted;


2)           
that the Council remains within all Prudential Indicators set for
itself for the year (see paragraphs 4.87 to 4.88 and Appendix L) be
noted;


3)           
the significant financial challenges facing the Council and the
need to identify further in year mitigations to reduce the forecast
overspend be noted;


4)           
the transfer of S106 funding to the NHS for improvements at
Willaston Surgery (see paragraph 4.16)
be approved; and


5)           
an increase of £0.5m in the Capital Programme for a scheme at
Lache Community Centre (see paragraph 4.17) be approved.
 
Reason for
Decision
 
To ensure the Council remains a well-managed
authority, recognising and responding to emerging cost pressures
and complying with current accounting requirements.
 
Alternative
Options
 
The report sets out various recommendations.
Members could choose not to approve the recommendations. However,
this is not recommended as this would adversely impact the
Council’s financial position.

Cabinet considered the report of the Assistant
Chief Executive which set out the Council’s performance in
relation to the missions set out in the ‘Play your part in a
stronger future’ Borough Plan 2024-2028.  The report provided an assessment of progress
against the key activities and milestones, performance measures and
targets set out in the Annual Delivery Plan, and assessed the
Council’s progress towards achieving the Borough Plan
missions. The report covered performance over period one of the
financial year, from 1 April 2026 to 31 July 2026.
 
Councillor Louise Gittins, Leader of the
Council, led the discussion on the item as proposer and the item
was seconded by Councillor Stuart Bingham, Cabinet Member for
Community Safety and
Neighbourhood Pride
 
Members noted that overall
performance against the Council’s Borough Plan remained
positive, with the majority of measures and actions on track or
meeting targets across all six missions. 
 
Cabinet Members took the opportunity
to highlight some of the key headlines, achievements, areas of
positive performance and also challenges within their individual
portfolios. Briefly, areas of strong performance included
children’s services reforms, the Starting Well
programme, adult social care assessments and the work carried out
to deliver the Contaminated Land Strategy and Local Nature
Strategy.
 
Members further noted that key
challenges remained around the number of children in residential
care, SEND and Education Health and Care Plan timeliness, road
repair performance and the delivery of a small number of delayed
programmes. Members also acknowledged that fly tipping rates had
increased for the first quarter from the previous year.
 
Despite these pressures,
Members were reassured that Borough Plan missions were generally
progressing well, with significant regeneration, community
investment and service improvement activity continuing across the
borough.
 
Visiting Members: Councillor Simon Eardley spoke in
relation to this item and Councillor Charles
Hardy spoke on behalf of Councillor Adrian Waddelove in relation to
this item.
 
Cabinet welcomed the report and thanked Council
officers across all services for all they did, constantly
responding and adapting to changing demands and need in their
service area, to ensure continuous improvement for all residents of
the Borough. 
 
DECIDED:     That
 

1)           
the performance of the Council at period one (1 April 2026 to 31
July 2026) against the missions set out in the ‘Play your
part in a stronger future’ Borough Plan 2024-28 be
noted;


2)           
the amended measure on the timeliness of road repairs as described
in paragraph 4.40 be approved; and


3)           
the Council’s Overview and Scrutiny Committees be provided
with the performance information set out in the report so that they
can understand and challenge performance and consider using it to
inform scrutiny work programmes across all committees.
 
Reason for
Decision
 
To ensure that up to date performance
information is available to enable the Cabinet, other Members,
senior Council officers and the public to understand progress
against the Borough Plan. This includes work being undertaken to
address any areas of challenge, and to support any necessary
discussions about reallocating resources to better achieve the
missions set out within the Borough Plan.
 
Alternative
Options
 
The report includes recommendations. Members
could choose not to approve the recommendations. However, this
could adversely impact future performance and so it is not
recommended.

Cabinet considered the confidential report of
the Director of Education and Inclusion concerning the acquisition

Councillor Adam Langan, Cabinet Member for

the recommendations as set out in section 2 of

As set out in section 3 of the confidential

Alternative
Options
 
As set out in section 13 of the confidential
report.

The report is seeking approval for the
proposed ‘prescribed
alteration’ to Greenbank School (the School) to permanently discontinue (close) the
residential provision at Greenbank School, Northwich.
content:
The report is seeking approval for the
proposed ‘prescribed
alteration’ to Greenbank School (the School) to permanently discontinue (close) the
residential provision at Greenbank School, Northwich.

That the permanent discontinuance (closure) of
the residential provision at Greenbank School, Northwich be
approved.

1)          
The proposal
is a response to the request by the Governing Body of the school to
undertake the process of closure of its residential provision as
set out in 
statutory guidance.
 
2)          
While
acknowledging that residential provision is valued by pupils and
families, the school recognised following the end of the Extended
Day/Residential funding grant that supported the residential
provision, it would become increasingly unaffordable to maintain
from the schools delegated budget. The governing body recognised
that any proposal affecting residential provision may be of concern
to pupils, families and staff. As such, the school carried out an
informal consultation between 8 June and 6 July 2026 seeking views
on the proposal and allowing an opportunity for stakeholders to
understand the rationale for the proposal and to share their views
before any formal statutory process was considered.
 
3)          
The School
and its Governing Board wished to not only maintain the
current

provision but also re-establish provision to 2013
levels. Following the decision by the Council to discontinue the
Extended Day/Residential funding grant, the school considered the
feasibility of whether the provision should continue to operate via
existing budgets/alternative funding or cease in its entirety. The
Council signposted the school to other funding opportunities as
part of discussions. The school outlined if it were to fund only
the current residential provision and retain the minimum staffing
structure to run and manage residential safely and effectively, by
2027-28 the school budget would be in deficit. A deficit that would
progressively worsen in the years afterwards, thereby materially
affecting meeting the needs of the main student body. In the
absence of any alternative funding streams the school concluded to
progress the proposal for closure of the provision from August
2026.

 
4)          
At the
request of the governing body the Council carried out a formal
consultation (Notice and representation period) between 14 July and
11 August 2026 proposing closure of the provision.

There are no further
options appropriate for this proposal.

services to the Council, or on its behalf. As part of its
governance arrangements, the Council retains a
number of powers which enable it to ensure these companies
continue to operate in ways that support the Council's strategic
priorities and objectives.
 

2)           
One of
the key controls is the requirement for each company to produce an
Annual Business Plan (ABP) which is reviewed and approved by the
Council in its role as shareholder.
 

3)           
This
report seeks shareholder approval for the 2026–27 Annual
Business Plans for Brio, Cheshire West Recycling Limited (CWR),

report also summarises the scrutiny process undertaken as part of
the Council's governance arrangements and highlights the key

1)   
the 2026-27 Annual Business Plans of the following Council
Companies be approved:

Cheshire West and Chester Leisure CIC (trading as Brio Leisure)
·        
Cheshire West Recycling Limited (CWR)
·        
Avenue Services (NW) Limited
·        
Edsential CIC

the findings and recommendations arising from the Council Companies

The proposals set out in the Business Plans help to ensure that the
companies' strategic plans remain aligned to the Council's core
priorities and Borough Plan objectives.


2)           
The Business Plans have been reviewed through the Council's
shareholder governance arrangements and pre-decision scrutiny

the Council Companies Scrutiny Task Group and Overview and Scrutiny

are therefore recommended for approval.

Capital Programme:

The report is seeking approval for the
proposed ‘prescribed
alteration’ to Archers Brook School (the School) to
permanently discontinue (close) the residential provision at
Archers Brook Social, Emotional and Mental Health (SEMH)
Residential School, Ellesmere Port.
content:
The report is seeking approval for the
proposed ‘prescribed
alteration’ to Archers Brook School (the School) to
permanently discontinue (close) the residential provision at
Archers Brook Social, Emotional and Mental Health (SEMH)
Residential School, Ellesmere Port.

That the permanent
discontinuance (closure) of the residential provision at Archers
Brook Social, Emotional and Mental Health (SEMH) Residential
School, Ellesmere Port be approved.


(1)         
The proposal
is a response to the request by the Governing Body of the school to
undertake the process of closure of its residential provision as
set out in 
statutory guidance.


(2)         
The
Governing Body carried out an informal consultation between 28
February and 4 April 2025 proposing the closure of its residential
provision would allow the school to redirect facilities to sustain
and enhance its core educational offer. While acknowledging that
residential provision is valued by pupils and families, the school
highlighted that it has become increasingly unaffordable and
heavily reliant on a grant that has not met operational costs for
several years.


(3)         
The
Governing Body believes the provision is no longer financially
viable within the school’s delegated budget,
citing:
 
·        
Loss of
commissioned services funding from the Council in August
2026
·        
Increasing
complexity of pupil needs
·        
Lack of
value for money in maintaining the provision
 

(4)         
The Council
agrees with the Governing Body that the current level of need
presents significant challenges to the long-term sustainability and
value for money of the provision and carried out a formal
consultation (Notice and representation period) between 11 June and
9 July 2026. 

There are no further
options appropriate for this proposal.
topline: The Children and Young People Portfolio Holder has decided to permanently discontinue the residential provision at Archers Brook SEMH Residential School in Ellesmere Port.

content:
Cabinet considered the report of the Director
of Economy and Housing concerning the preparation of a Local Plan,
the key document to guide development across the borough over a
minimum 15-year period.  The report
provided an update on the transition to a new plan-making system
and sought approval to delegate plan-making functions to enable a
Local Plan to be adopted as soon as possible.
 
Members were reminded that local authorities
were required to move to the new plan-making process which was
intended to create a clearer, faster and more streamlined route to
adopting Local Plans, with a target timescale of around 30 months
from the early stages of preparation to adoption. Members’
attention was drawn to sections 4.8 to 4.12 in the report which
outlined the three mandatory Gateway stages introduced by the
Government, intended to ensure the plans were robust,
evidence-based and capable of withstanding examination. 
 
Members noted the process which had already
commenced and that the Council had published its timetable with the
intention of submitting the Local Plan for examination by May 2028
and achieving adoption by December 2028.
 
Visiting Members: Councillor Martin Loftus
spoke in relation to the item. 
 
Councillor Christine Warner, Cabinet Member
for Homes and Planning, led the discussion on the item as proposer
and the item was seconded by Councillor Karen Shore, Cabinet Member
for Transport and Highways (including Waste).
 
Councillor Warner outlined the composition of
the new expanded Local Plan Working Group, explaining that she had
considered the geography of the whole borough as well as urban and
rural areas when inviting additional members to be represented on
that group.
 
Cabinet Members welcomed the report and the
timely update and supported the transition to the new plan-making
system. They acknowledged that an up to date Local Plan was
essential as, without one, the Council was more vulnerable to
speculative development and had less control over where growth took
place.
 
DECIDED:     That 
 

1)           
the move to the new system and the publication of the notice of
intention to commence preparation be noted;


2)           
 the publication of the Local Plan
timetable and arrangements in place for the Local Plan Working
Group be noted;


3)           
 the Cabinet Member for Homes and
Planning be delegated authority:

·        
to agree the content and arrangements for the Regulation 20 Scoping
Consultation;
·        
to agree the content and arrangements for the Regulation 23 plan
content and evidence consultation;
·        
to issue a notice to commence any supplementary plans and ensure
the necessary requirements are met for adoption;
·        
to make changes to the process for preparing the Local Plan or a
Supplementary Plan to ensure compliance with legal
requirements;
 

4)           
the Head of Planning and Placemaking be delegated authority:
 
·        
to approve, submit and publish documents, including consultation
summaries, required for and following Gateway assessments;
·        
to, in consultation with the Cabinet Member, revise and publish the
local plan timetable;
·        
to consult on and publish documents required to meet Strategic
Environmental Assessment, Habitat Regulations Assessment or other
required assessments;
·        
to publish and consult on evidence base; and
·        
to publish and consult on policy background papers.
 
Reason for
Decision 
 
To ensure the Council meets its statutory
requirement to adopt a Local Plan within the appropriate
timeframe.
 
Alternative
Options
 
The Council is required to prepare a new Local
Plan within the timescales set out by Government. The report
outlines measures to help ensure the process is as carried out
efficiently and effectively as possible.
topline: The Council has decided to delegate plan-making functions to enable the adoption of a Local Plan to guide development across the borough.

purpose:
Cabinet is asked to approve the
commission of the Healthy Child Programme and the In-house Delivery
of the Children’s Centre Core Offer.
content:
Cabinet is asked to approve the
commission of the Healthy Child Programme and the In-house Delivery
of the Children’s Centre Core Offer.

Cabinet considered the report of the Director
of Public Health and the Executive Director of Children and
Families concerning proposals for the future delivery of early
years and children’s health services across the borough. This
included removal of the Children’s Centre Core Offer from the
current Starting Well contract to bring it back in-house from July
2027, and to recommission the Healthy Child Programme as a
standalone service through a competitive process.  The report also outlined the feedback from the
engagement on the Starting Well service and the consultation on the
Healthy Child Programme as well as the proposed changes.
 
Members noted that the proposals responded to
national reforms and the Council’s ambition to develop Best
Start Family Hubs, particularly in the most disadvantaged
communities.  Members’ attention
was drawn to the extensive engagement undertaken with families,
young people and partners as part of a 12-week boroughwide
consultation from November 2025 to February 2026, with the findings
from the engagement attached at appendix C.  Whilst Members noted the additional investment
required in order to deliver the new model, they noted it would
ensure compliance with national funding requirements and would
provide a more integrated, flexible and sustainable model of
support, aligned with national policy and local priorities.
 
Councillor Lisa Denson, Cabinet Member for A
Fairer Future, led the discussion on the item as proposer and the
item was seconded by Councillor Adam Langan, Cabinet Member for
Children and Young People.
 
Members welcomed the report and the proposals
and acknowledged the work of the current provider, Cheshire and
Wirral Partnership NHS Trust.  Members
felt that by bringing the Children’s Centre Core Offer
in-house, this would strengthen integration with Early Support and
Family Help, improve flexibility, and support delivery of the
Family Hub model.
 
DECIDED:     That 
 

1)           
the expenditure of £1.092m required in order to fund the
delivery of the Children’s Centre Core Offer by the Council
rather than an external provider be approved;


2)           
the proposal to recommission a standalone Healthy Child Programme,
at an annual value of £6.580m (which includes additional
expenditure of £0.200m referred to in paragraph 7.2 of the
report) be approved;


3)           
the Director of Public Health, in consultation with the Director of
Finance and Portfolio Holder for A Fairer Future (Poverty, Public
Health and Mental Health), be delegated authority to award the
Healthy Child Programme contract to the successful provider
following the competitive process;


4)           
the Director of Public Health, in consultation with the Director of
Finance, be delegated authority to agree the final Healthy Child
Programme contract value for the duration of the contract, which
will be dependent on the Public Health Grant allocation;
and


5)           
the Director of Public Health, in consultation with the Director of
Finance and the Portfolio Holder for A Fairer Future (Poverty,
Public Health and Mental Health) be delegated authority to agree
any “in contract” changes relating to service provision
or financial value that may be required during the Healthy Child
Programme contract period (with any changes being no greater than
£1m).
 
Reason for
Decision
 

1)           
Recent reforms in Children’s Services require
multi-disciplinary teams to be delivered through Best Start Family
Hubs in the most deprived areas of the borough. To enable this
model and ensure the Early Support Service can effectively manage
access to and use of Family Hub spaces, it is recommended that the
Children’s Centre Core Offer is brought in-house and the
Healthy Child Programme is commissioned as a standalone service
(see paragraphs 4.2–4.4). This approach will strengthen the
Council’s ability to deliver integrated, accessible and
flexible support for families, improve alignment with Early Support
services and national policy, and contribute to improved outcomes.
These recommendations support progress towards the statutory Early
Years Foundation Stage target, that by 2028, 75.5% of 5 year olds
have a good level of development, 52.5% for those on Free School
Meals (FSM), relative to a current position of 67.7% overall and
45.1% FSM.


2)           
The recommendation to commission the HCP contract through a
competitive PSR process aims to secure a high-quality, robust and
cost-effective service that meets the Council’s statutory
duty. A long-term approach will secure a consistent service and
offer increased stability for service delivery, reflecting feedback
from engagement with families, young people, and partners.
 
Alternative
Options
 

1)           
The services could continue to be commissioned as part of an
integrated service that includes both the HCP and the
Children’s Centre Core Offer. However, changes to Department
for Education policy, directing councils to establish Best Start
Family Hubs, have encouraged a re-consideration of the delivery
model for the Children’s Centre Core Offer. Establishment of
Best Start Family Hubs calls on the Council to play an
orchestrating role, bringing together multiple services. Bringing
the centres in house will allow the Council to manage the space
within and accessibility of the Best Start Family Hubs and
Children’s Centres.


2)           
A robust options appraisal has been undertaken which considered the
cost and risks for the alternative option of bringing the HCP in
house as opposed to commissioning the service. The in-house option
has been fully appraised and is not recommended due to the higher
annual costs and the considerable cost of the IT system (up to
£3m) based on the small number of local authorities who have
taken similar steps. There are also significant clinical governance
risks associated with bringing this service in-house including
reduced access to NHS clinical governance infrastructure,
professional isolation and weaker integration with NHS
services.


3)           
It is unlikely that a third party commissioned provider would be
able to achieve greater value for money in delivering the
Children’s Centre Core Offer than either an integrated
service or in-house service. A standalone commission would require
a separate management team, instead of sharing management with
other services as happens now or under the proposed model. A
standalone management structure would be more costly than sharing
management with existing in-house Early Support services.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the commission of the Healthy Child Programme and bring the Children’s Centre Core Offer in-house, following extensive engagement and consultation.

purpose:
The report to Cabinet will present the
recommendations for procuring a new contract to deliver repairs and
maintenance, void, and gas servicing and compliance works in
support of the Housing Management Service. Cabinet is requested to
approve the commencement of the procurement process for this
contract.
content:
The report to Cabinet will present the
recommendations for procuring a new contract to deliver repairs and
maintenance, void, and gas servicing and compliance works in
support of the Housing Management Service. Cabinet is requested to
approve the commencement of the procurement process for this
contract.

Cabinet considered the report of the Director
of Economy and Housing which sought approval to commence the
re-procurement of a new suite of contracts for the delivery of
repairs, maintenance, voids (empty property) and gas servicing and
compliance works and services to support the Council Housing
Management Service.
 
Members noted that the procurement formed part
of a wider programme to strengthen and modernise its housing
services following the return of housing management functions to
direct Council control in April 2026. 
The current repairs, maintenance and voids contract was delivered
by Liberty (due to end on 31st March 2027) and the current gas servicing and compliance
contract was delivered by Liberty Gas (due to end on
30th June 2027).  It was
further noted that the Council intended to use an established
procurement framework, such as Fusion21 (UK based social enterprise
delivering compliant public sector procurement frameworks with
embedded social value) to support the re-procurement. This would
enable the Council to undertake a mini-competition process tailored
to specific priorities and would provide flexibility to place
emphasis on key areas such as social value and tenant engagement,
ensuring that these elements were embedded within the procurement
and delivery of the contracts.
 
Councillor Christine Warner, Cabinet Member
for Homes and Planning, led the discussion on the item as proposer
and the item was seconded by Councillor Paul Donovan, Cabinet
Member for Democracy, Workforce and Communities.
 
Cabinet Members welcomed the report and
supported the proposals, highlighting that tenants could be
confident and reassured that they would continue to receive safe,
reliable and high-quality maintenance services. 
 
DECIDED:     That 
 

1)           
the re-procurement of the repairs & maintenance and void
contract be approved, to ensure continuity of essential services
beyond the current contract term;


2)           
the re-procurement of the gas servicing and electrical compliance
contract be approved, to ensure continuity of essential services
beyond the current contract term;


3)           
a contract extension of the Liberty R&M Contract be approved
for 6-months to 30th September 2027, with a contract
value for 6 months being approximately £3.3m; and


4)           
the Director of Economy and Housing, in consultation with the
Cabinet Member for Homes and Planning, be delegated authority to
undertake an appropriate procurement process including contract

and contract mobilisation of services to be delivered by the

Reason for
Decision 
 
As set out in detail in section 3 of the
report (paragraphs 3.1 to 3.4).
 
Alternative
Options
 

1)           
The current two contracts remain in place and includes an option to extend for a further two
years, allowing service continuation until 2029. This option is not

2)           
For the reasons set out in this report the recommendation is to

content:
The draft Strategy sets out the
Council’s approach to dealing with land affected by
contamination which is located in all areas of the borough as a
result of its industrial heritage and previous lack of
regulation.

Cabinet considered the report of the Director
of Environment and Communities which sought approval of the draft
Cheshire West and Chester Contaminated Land Strategy 2026-2031
(attached at appendix 1).
 
Members noted that the Council had a statutory
duty under Part IIA of the Environment Act 1990 to set out in
writing its approach to carrying out its inspection duty for the
purpose of identifying potentially contaminated land sites within
the borough and determine whether they meet the statutory
definition of contaminated land.  The
Council’s approach was set out in the draft Contaminated Land
Strategy which was attached as Appendix 1.
 
Members’ attention was drawn to section
4 of the report which detailed how the strategy was developed as
well as the robust 12-week consultation which was undertaken from
November 2025 to February 2026.  The
consultation feedback report was attached at appendix
2.  Members also noted that a progress
report on development of the draft Strategy had been considered by
Places Overview and Scrutiny Committee in October 2025 and that two
members of the Committee had joined the cross-party Contaminated
Land Member Task and Finish Group which carried out a review of the
draft Strategy prior to it going out to public consultation.
 
Councillor Stuart Bingham, Cabinet Member for
Community Safety and Neighbourhood Pride, led the discussion on the
item as proposer and the item was seconded by Councillor Karen
Shore, Cabinet Member for Transport and Highways (including
Waste).
 
Cabinet Members welcomed the report and the
draft Contaminated Land Strategy, highlighting it as a significant
and important piece of work which every local authority must have
in place.  It was recognised that the
Council had gone into greater detail than what was statutorily
required when developing the draft Strategy.  Members welcomed the comprehensive consultation
undertaken and highlighted the strong support shown in the
consultation for the polluter pays principle, that the polluter
should bear the cost of remediating contamination.  Councillor Bingham thanked all involved in the
development of the Strategy including officers, Councillors and
partner organisations, and in particular everyone who responded to
the consultation which ultimately helped shape the Strategy and
ensure it was compliant and tailored to local need.
 
DECIDED:     That 
 
the draft Contaminated Land Strategy 2026-2031
(attached as appendix 1 to the report) be approved.
 
Reason for
Decision 
 
To ensure that the Council complies with its
obligations under Part IIA of the Environmental Protection Act 1990
and associated statutory guidance.
 
Alternative
Options
 
It is an option not to publish a Contaminated
Land Strategy in which case the Council would not be fulfilling its
statutory duty.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the draft Cheshire West and Chester Contaminated Land Strategy 2026-2031 to comply with environmental protection laws.

content:
Cabinet considered the report of the Director
of Economy and Housing which sought approval for the making of
non-immediate Article 4 Directions, to remove permitted development
rights for change of use from Class E (commercial, business and
service class) to C3 (dwellinghouses) at Chester Business Park,
part of Chester West / Sealand Industrial Estate and Gadbrook Park Northwich. The proposed areas to
which the Directions related were attached at appendices 1, 2 and 3
to the report.
 
Members noted that the proposals were intended
to protect strategically important employment areas from the
continued loss of office and business space and to ensure that
future changes of use were subject to full planning
assessment.  This was felt necessary in
areas where there was evidence of significant pressure for
residential conversion and where the loss of commercial premises
could have a detrimental impact on local employment opportunities,
investment and economic growth.  Members
further noted that the approach aimed to provide a balanced
response to protecting business growth and investment whilst
maintaining appropriate opportunities for housing development in
suitable locations.
 
Councillor Christine Warner, Cabinet Member
for Homes and Planning, led the discussion on the item as proposer
and the item was seconded by Councillor Nathan Pardoe, Cabinet
Member for Inclusive Economy, Regeneration and Digital
Transformation.
 
Cabinet Members welcomed the report and the
proposals to help the Council protect business areas and employment
in a targeted and evidence-led way. 
They highlighted that this was not about preventing development,
but rather about giving full consideration to the wider impact of
potential development.  Members thanked
officers for the comprehensive report and also the public speaker
for her comments and support.
 
DECIDED:     That 
 

1)           
the making of three non-immediate Article 4 Directions to remove
the permitted development rights ordinarily allowed under Class MA,
Part 3 of Schedule 2 of the GPDO 2015 (as amended by the 2019
Regulations) for “Development consisting of a change of
use of a building and any land within its curtilage from a use
falling within Class E (commercial, business and service) of
Schedule 2 to the Use Classes Order to a use falling within Class
C3 (dwellinghouses)” be approved, relating to:
 
·        
Chester Business Park as shown in Appendix 1
·        
Chester West / Sealand Industrial Estate as shown in Appendix 2
·        
Gadbrook Park as shown in Appendix
3
 

2)           
the consultation and notification procedure to be carried out be
noted.
 
Reason for
Decision 
 

1)           
The making of the Article 4 Directions will enable the Council, as
the Local Planning Authority (“LPA”) to use its
planning powers to ensure there is an appropriate balance of uses
in the defined employment areas, to support local employment
opportunities and to ensure development proposals are considered in
accordance with the adopted Local Plan. The adopted Local Plan
(Part One) identifies the strategic importance of these areas as
employment areas through policies STRAT 3 (safeguarding Chester
Business Park and Chester West / Sealand Industrial Estate) and
STRAT 5 (protecting Gadbrook Park for
continued employment use). Residential development in these
strategic employment locations could result in wholly unacceptable
adverse impacts for local businesses and limit new investment
opportunities. There is also the need to ensure residential
development is delivered in a way that builds cohesive communities
and meets the required space standards for residential
development.


2)           
The Article 4 Directions mean that a particular development cannot
be carried out under permitted development rights and a planning
application approved by the LPA would be required to make the
change. An Article 4 Direction does not prohibit development but
enables the Local Planning Authority to have some control over the
proposed development and consider it in more detail. The
recommendations are sought to ensure any future proposals for
residential development in these strategic employment areas, are
assessed in line with the Council’s adopted development
plan. 
 
Alternative
Options
 

1)           
An alternative option would be to take forward Article 4 Directions
with immediate effect for Chester Business Park, part of Chester
West / Sealand Industrial Estate or Gadbrook Park. The supporting evidence report
suggest that Gadbrook Park would be the
priority. The key differences being the Article 4 would come into
effect immediately and the risk of compensation claims could be
high. In proceeding via a non-immediate Article 4, PD will be able
to continue without LPA control within the 12 month period and as
such delay planning control in the defined areas.


2)           
Other employment areas have been assessed through the Supporting
Evidence Report (2026), but the report suggests that these sites
support lower levels of employment and GVA, meaning that any
potential loss of floorspace would have a more limited and have a
largely non-strategic economic impact.


3)           
There is an option for no change/do nothing at the present time.
This is not recommended as it would not provide the ability for the
LPA to effectively assess proposals against the Council’s
adopted development plan. It could undermine the economic function
of the strategic employment locations identified. It would also
mean that the Council would not be able to manage the location,
size, tenure mix or quality of new housing being produced through
this form of permitted development.
topline: The Council has decided to approve non-immediate Article 4 Directions to protect strategic employment areas from residential conversion, balancing business growth and housing development.

purpose:
To inform Members of the
financial performance of the Council for the 2025-26 financial
year. Members are asked to approve any proposed changes to the
capital programme and revenue budget.
content:
To inform Members of the
financial performance of the Council for the 2025-26 financial
year. Members are asked to approve any proposed changes to the
capital programme and revenue budget.

Cabinet considered the report of the Director
of Finance which set out the financial performance of the Council
for the 2025-26 financial year. This covered the 12-month period
from 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026 and summarised the key headlines
for financial performance, covering revenue and capital
budgets.
 
Councillor Carol Gahan, Cabinet Member for
Finance and Legal, led the discussion on the item as proposer and
the item was seconded by Councillor Louise Gittins, Leader of the
Council.
 
Councillor Gahan highlighted key headlines
within the report on the Council’s financial position. She
reported that for the 2025-26 financial year, the Council had an
overspend of £1.1m against its approved budget. Whilst spend
had not been contained within the approved budget, the level of
overspend had reduced during the year, from the forecast
£6.9m pressure (after planned mitigations) reported to
Cabinet in January 2026. She reported that whilst it was positive
that the level of overspend had reduced during the year, there were
continued significant cost pressures in Adults Services which had
caused a final outturn pressure of £12.8m within the
directorate.  However, Childrens Services had reported a £1.8m
underspend, with the number of children in care reducing, however
the number of high cost placements was above the budgeted figure
and remained a key risk area for the Council due to its
volatility.
 
Councillor Gahan further reported that as a
result of the pressures mentioned, the Council had to identify
significant mitigating actions in year from across
all directorates and council-wide budgets to offset the pressure.
The Council also utilised underspends on capital financing, driven
by interest earnt on cash balances and reduced borrowing. In
addition, the Council extended the Flexible Use of Capital Receipts
for Transformation by £2.0m. 
 
Members noted that the £1.1m overspend for 2025-26 reduced the
general fund reserve to £24.1m, which fell below the
Council’s risk assessed range of £24.9m to
£27.9m. However, the 2026-27 budget included a planned
contribution of £3.0m to the General Fund reserve which would
replenish the reserve to within the Council’s risk arranged
range.
 
Visiting Members: Councillor Charles Hardy
spoke in relation to the item. 
 
Cabinet Members welcomed the comprehensive
report detailing the Council’s financial position, noting
that it had been considered at Cheshire West and Chester Overview
and Scrutiny Committee on 6th July 2026.  Members further noted that, due to positive and
proactive actions, the Council had been
able to mitigate a significant proportion of the financial
pressures in-year. They recognised that pressures remained,
particularly within Adult Social Care, and that the challenges
would likely continue to be significant.  The formation of the cross-party Adult Social Care
Budget Member Working Group was highlighted and welcomed in order
to investigate the challenges in this area and strengthen
transparency, understanding and member
oversight of the Adult Social Care budget.
 
Members thanked the Finance team for the
comprehensive report and for its continued robust financial
management which meant the council was in a better position
compared to that of neighbouring local authorities.
 
DECIDED:     That 
 
Revenue Budget:
 

1)           
the overall financial position of a £1.1m overspend and the
call on the General Reserve be noted;


2)           
the carry forward of revenue budgets
within directorates (£0.1m) and central budgets (£0.4m)
to support planned spend in 2026-27 (paragraph 4.12) be
noted;


3)           
the Council remains within all Prudential Indicators set for itself
for the year (see paragraphs 4.87 to 4.88 and Appendix L) be noted;
and
 
Capital Programme:
 

4)           
the capital programme delivery and key outputs for 2025-26 (see
paragraphs 4.15 to 4.20 and detailed in appendices) be noted.
 
Reason for
Decision 
 
To ensure the Council remains a well-managed
authority, recognising and responding to emerging cost pressures
and complying with current accounting requirements.
 
Alternative
Options
 
The report sets out various recommendations.
Members could choose not to approve the recommendations. However,
this is not recommended as this would adversely impact the
Council’s financial position.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to address the £1.1m overspend in the Council's 2025-26 financial year through significant mitigating actions.

content:
Cabinet considered the report of the Assistant
Chief Executive which set out the Council’s performance in
relation to the six missions set out in the ‘Play your part
in a stronger future’ Borough Plan 2024-2028. This report
focused on performance over period four of the financial year, from
1 December 2025 to 31 March 2026.
 
Councillor Louise Gittins, Leader of the
Council, led the discussion on the item as proposer and the item
was seconded by Councillor Nathan Pardoe, Cabinet Member for
Inclusive Economy, Regeneration and Digital Transformation.
 
Councillor Gittins explained that the report
set out the performance against key indicators and highlighted
graph 1 (section 4.2) with 81 indicators showing as green, 15
showing as amber and 34 showing as red in relation to overall
performance at year end. In addition, graph 2 (section 4.3) set out
a summary of measure performance against target at year end, with
36 actions green, 8 actions amber and 29 actions red. Members noted
the report had been considered at Cheshire West and Chester
Overview & Scrutiny Committee on 6th July
2026.  Members were encouraged to drill
down into the missions detailed in the appendices where each of the
missions were assessed as progressing well, with the majority of
actions and measures showing as green against target.
 
Councillor Gittins highlighted some positive
areas of performance with the missions, in particular in the
‘Starting Well’ mission the reducing rate of Children
in Care which had fallen from 83 in March 2025 to 75 in 2026, the
lowest rate since 2022.  In the
‘Tackling Hardship and Poverty’ mission there were 900
homelessness preventions which was increasing year on year and the
number of homeless households in temporary accommodation remained
green.  Within ‘Resilient people
living their best lives’, the number of carers assessments
was continuing to grow, as was the number of visits to Brio Leisure
Centres for physical activity.  Within
the ‘Opportunity in a fair local economy’ mission,
Councillor Gittins highlighted the number of people supported by
the Council to start or stay in work as well as placement support
for young people. Finally, under the ‘Neighbourhood
Pride’ mission, there had been significant work to ensure
private rented sector properties were safe and healthy places to
live and 188,488 trees had been planted.
 
Visiting Members: Councillors Charles Hardy
(on behalf of Councillor Adrian Waddelove) and Simon Eardley spoke in relation to
the item.
 
Cabinet Members welcomed the report and took
the opportunity to highlight some of the key headlines,
achievements and areas of positive performance within their
individual portfolios which were all detailed in the
appendices.  Councillor Gittins also
took the opportunity to highlight the Performance Highlights
webpage on the Council’s website at: 
Performance Highlights 25-26 | CWC Borough Plan which
publicly reported on performance progress and included a range of
video stories which brought to life the human element of the
performance data and the impact on residents.
 
DECIDED:     That 
 

1)           
the performance of the Council at period four (1 December 2025 to
31 March 2026) against the missions set out in the ‘Play your
part in a stronger future’ Borough Plan 2024-28 be noted;
and


2)           
the Council’s Overview and Scrutiny Committees be provided
with the performance information set out in the report so that they
can understand and challenge performance and consider using it to
inform scrutiny work programmes across all committees.
 
Reason for
Decision 
 
To ensure that up to date performance
information is available to enable the Cabinet, other Members,
senior Council officers and the public to understand progress
against the Borough Plan. This includes work being undertaken to
address any areas of challenge, and to support any necessary
discussions about reallocating resources to better achieve the
missions set out within the Borough Plan.
 
Alternative
Options
 
The report includes recommendations. Members
could choose not to approve the recommendations. However, this
could adversely impact future performance and so it is not
recommended.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the performance of the Council against the missions set out in the 'Play your part in a stronger future' Borough Plan 2024-28.

which set out the major strategic actions and projects which will

DECIDED:     That

Decision

To provide a clear summary of the programme of activity which the

2)           
To provide a clear framework of measures and targets that can be

To support regular performance reporting of activity and
impact.

Options

content:
Cabinet considered the report of the Director
of Transport and Highways which sought authority to submit a
funding bid to the Department for Transport (DfT) Structures Fund
to carry out repair works to Nicholas Street Viaduct and Winsford
Station bridge.
 
Members noted that the Fund was a DfT capital
grant programme which was launched in April 2026 to support the
repair, strengthening and replacement of existing local highway
structures including bridges, tunnels, flyovers and associated
assets. The deadline for submission of full business cases was
3rd August 2026, and funding decisions were expected to
be announced in Autumn 2026. Successful schemes would be required
to complete all funded works by March 2030.  Should the bid be successful, which was for grant
valued at up to £37.3 million, there would be an element of
matching contribution by the council of up to £4.15
million.
 
Visiting Members: Councillor Simon Eardley
spoke in relation to the item. 
 
Councillor Karen Shore, Cabinet Member for
Transport and Highways (including Waste), led the discussion on the
item as proposer and the item was seconded by Councillor Carol
Gahan, Cabinet Member for Finance and Legal.
 
Cabinet Members welcomed the opportunity to
submit a bid to this funding programme and recognised the hard work
of officers as part of their ongoing inspection and investigation
works. Members were mindful of the potential network rail
disruption any repair works and further investigations would bring.
It was also acknowledged that there were other structures in a
similar position and the expected costs of repair meant that
significant repair works could not be delivered under the existing
Council capital budget for structures. 
Members were keen to put forward future bids should there be a
‘round two’ programme and thanked officers for their
hard work in preparing the report and the bid and hoped it would be
successful.
 
DECIDED:     That 
 

1)           
the submission of a grant funding bid to the Department for
Transport’s Structures Fund, seeking up to £37.3
million of grant funding to enable remedial works at key highways
sites in Chester and Winsford be approved;


2)           
if successful, note that the bid will require the Council to match
fund that investment with up to £4.15 million of Council
resources from the funding set aside for this purpose in the
capital programme; and


3)           
the Director of Transport and Highways, in consultation with the
Director of Finance and S151 Officer, be delegated authority to
submit the funding bid as set out in this report and accept the
grant funding should the bid be successful.
 
Reason for
Decision 
 

1)           
The Council owns a large portfolio of highways structures that need
to be managed and maintained. Both Nicholas Street Viaduct and
Winsford Station bridge have been highlighted as the highest risk
Council owned structures in need of major maintenance.


2)           
In February 2025, the Council allocated an increased capital budget
to allow detailed post tensioned special inspections and Principal
Inspections to be carried out on these structures, which have
identified critical issues and increased the risk rating,
reinforcing the need for major maintenance. Post tensioned bridges
contain high strength steel tendons embedded within the concrete
structure. A post tensioned special inspection is required to
locate and view the condition of the steel tendons. Due to the
scale and complexity of the repairs required the cost cannot be
accommodated within the Council’s capital allocation.
Therefore, it is recommended additional streams of funding are
investigated.


3)           
The Department for Transport Structures Fund has recently been
announced and following a review of the funding criteria and the
Council risk review of structural assets, it is recommended that
bids for schemes of work to support the significant maintenance
required for both Nicholas Street Viaduct and Winsford Station
bridge are submitted.
 
Alternative
Options
 
It is believed that there are no feasible
alternative funding options and so the funding option set out in
this report is recommended.

Options considered:
 
Propose different
schemes: Based on the Funding criteria, the risk assessment of the
Council’s structures assets and the readiness of the schemes
to be delivered, it is considered these are the best two options to
put forward to the DfT for funding.

Do not issue the
submission. Not recommended as the works cannot be delivered within
current local funding, and delaying the works would increase the
risks of asset failure or the need to restrict usage.

Issue Scheme 1 but
not the Exceptional Scheme: It should be noted that development of
proposals for Winsford is not as far advanced as Nicholas St
Viaduct, however due to the significance and potential impact it is
proposed it is submitted as an exceptional scheme for DfT
consideration.
topline: The Council has decided to submit a funding bid for repair works on key highways sites in Chester and Winsford.

content:
(1)        
This report
reviews and makes
recommendations for an increase in the penaltylevels for
Fixed Penalty Notices
(FPNs) for
the environmentalcrime
offences of littering and fly
tipping (the illegal disposal of waste onto land that is not
licensed to accept it).


(2)        
The
report also outlines how FPNs could be
utilised as an alternative enforcement sanction for breaching the
household waste duty of care and makes recommendations on the
penalty levels.

That:
 

1)        
the Fixed Penalty Notice penalty level for the offence of littering
be increased to £150 for a lower-level littering offence,
while retaining the reduction for early payment within seven days
at £90;


2)        
that structured framework be introduced for littering offences, to
include an additional penalty level for a higher-level littering
offence as set out in paragraphs 4.5 and 4.6 and Table 2 of
Appendix 1 to the report;


3)        
the Fixed Penalty Notice penalty levels for fly tipping offences be
increased in accordance with the structured framework set out in
paragraph 4.6 and Table 4 of Appendix 1 to the report and include
the introduction of a reduced penalty for early payment in the case
of a higher-level offence;


4)        
the authority adopts a procedure for issuing Fixed Penalty Notices
for breaches of the
household waste duty of care; and


5)        
the Fixed Penalty Notice penalty levels for breaches of the
household waste duty of care be fixed in accordance with the
structured framework set out in paragraph 4.7 and Table 5 of
Appendix 1 to the report.


1)           
There are
significant environmental, social and financial impacts associated
with fly tipping and littering.  They
are a blight on local communities, a source of pollution, a
potential danger to public health and a hazard to
wildlife.  Reports of waste crime are
increasing, and the Council therefore needs to ensure the current
FPN penalty levels are appropriate for these offences, and act as
an effective deterrent.   


2)           
Following a
legislative amendment to the upper fixed penalty limit for the
offences of littering and fly tipping, the option to increase the
penalty levels has been carefully considered and is recommended.
Increasing the penalty for littering and introducing a penalty of a
higher-level littering offence and increasing the maximum penalty
for fly tipping offences from £400 to the statutory maximum
of £1,000 will send out a strong deterrent
message.  The introduction of FPNs for
breaches of the household waste duty of care will enhance the
authority’s effectiveness in dealing with this offence, by
speeding up the enforcement process, while maintaining a
proportionate and consistent approach. 


3)           
Maintaining
a distinction between higher- and lower-level offences of fly
tipping and breach of the household waste duty of care, and
introducing a distinction for littering offences, will ensure that
enforcement remains proportionate, and this approach, together with
the maintenance of a reduced penalty for early payment, will
encourage early and efficient disposal and mitigate against the
risk of non-payment.

It is an option not to increase the penalty
level for fly tipping and littering and not to introduce FPN
disposal for breaches of the household waste duty of
care.  This option is not recommended as
the number of offences remains high and there is a need for an
effective deterrent.
topline: The Community Safety and Neighbourhood Pride Portfolio Holder has decided to increase penalty levels for environmental crime offences in an effort to deter littering, fly tipping, and breaches of household waste duty of care.

content:
The draft Blacon
Community Neighbourhood Plan 2025-2040 and Blacon Community Neighbourhood Development Order
(“the Neighbourhood Plan and Neighbourhood Development
Order”) were submitted by Blacon Neighbourhood Alliance Neighbourhood Forum
(“the Forum”) to Cheshire West and Chester
Borough Council (“the Council”) in November
2025.  Following a seven-week publicity
period, the Neighbourhood Plan and Neighbourhood Development Order
were subjected to an independent examination. The reports of the
Examiner have been published and recommend that the Neighbourhood
Plan and Neighbourhood Development Order, once modified, proceeds
to referendum stage on the basis that they have met all the
relevant legal requirements. The Council as Local Planning
Authority (LPA) isrequired to consider each of the recommendations
made by the reports and decide how to proceed.

i)            
That the Examiner’s recommendations to make modifications to
the Neighbourhood Plan and Neighbourhood Development Order be
accepted and that the Neighbourhood Plan and Neighbourhood
Development Order will proceed to referendum in Summer 2026 be
approved.

 
ii)           
That delegation to the Head of Planning and Place Making to make
any necessary minor amendments to wording or formatting in the
Neighbourhood Plan and the Neighbourhood Development Order
following the decision to proceed to referendum be approved.

3.1. The LPA has a duty to provide advice and
assistance on Neighbourhood Plans and Neighbourhood Development
Orders to qualifying bodies to facilitate neighbourhood planning
(Schedule 4B Town and Country Planning Act 1990 (as amended)
(“the 1990 Act”)) and to make arrangements for a
referendum to take place following a favourable Examiner’s
report.
 
3.2. The Neighbourhood Plan and the
Neighbourhood Development Order have been prepared in accordance
with the procedural requirements as set out in the Neighbourhood
Planning (General) Regulations 2012 (SI 2012/637) (as amended)
(“the 2012 Regulations”). Subject to the modifications
set out in the Examiner’s report, the Neighbourhood Plan and
Neighbourhood Development Order are considered to meet the
necessary ‘Basic Conditions’ as set out in Paragraph
8(2) of Schedule 4B to the 1990 Act and can proceed to a referendum
at an appropriate time.

The other option is not to proceed to
referendum stage. However, without the referendum, the
Neighbourhood Plan would not form part of the statutory development
plan for the area and the Neighbourhood Development Order could not
be brought into force.
topline: The Homes and Planning Portfolio Holder has decided to accept modifications to the Blacon Community Neighbourhood Plan and Neighbourhood Development Order, proceeding to a referendum in Summer 2026.

purpose:
The purpose of the report is to seek Cabinet
approval of the new model for Smart Support which will replace the
current technology enabled care contract and to delegate authority
to the Executive Director of Adult Services to procure and award
the contract.
content:
The purpose of the report is to seek Cabinet
approval of the new model for Smart Support which will replace the
current technology enabled care contract and to delegate authority
to the Executive Director of Adult Services to procure and award
the contract.

Cabinet considered the report of the Executive
Director of Adult Services and the Executive Director of Children
and Families concerning proposed remodelling of the Council’s
current Technology Enabled Care (TEC) provision. The remodelled
service would use technology and digital care solutions which would
be all-age and borough wide and would take a strengths-based
approach for children and adults with eligible care needs,
complementing or reducing the need for more traditional care and
support. The current contract expires on 31 March 2027 and the
Council would use this opportunity to rename the current TEC
service to ‘Smart Support’, to reflect technological
advancements, and refine the service scope.
 
Members noted that the contract promoted
independence by providing individuals with digital support. This
included, but is not limited to, falls sensors, epilepsy sensors,
GPS watches, door sensors, medication dispensers and pendant alarms
as well as provision for remote support 24/7.
 
Members’ attention was also drawn to the
way in which Smart Support would support children, young people and
their families by ensuring that technology enabled solutions were
used as a preventative and enabling tool alongside statutory
Children’s Social Care, SEND and Early Help services. The
service would also support children and young people with
disabilities, special educational needs, long-term health
conditions and vulnerabilities, including those who are moving into
adulthood, to live safely at home, improve independence and reduce
reliance on more intrusive or high-cost interventions.
 
Visiting Members: Councillor Gaynor Sinar and
Charles Hardy spoke in relation to the item. 
 
Councillor Sheila Little, Cabinet Member for
Adult Social Care, led the discussion on the item as proposer and
the item was seconded by Councillor Carol Gahan, Cabinet Member for
Finance and Legal.
 
Cabinet Members welcomed the report and were
encouraged by the way in which an alliance would be formed, as part
of the commission, to ensure that future developments in technology
would be incorporated into the scheme. This would ensure that the
service remained up to date.
 
Members wished to place on record their thanks
to all staff who had been involved in the delivery of this proposal
as they continued to show commitment and dedication to improving
the lives of residents through preventative and supportive measures
to keep them well.
 
DECIDED:     That
 

1)           
the model for the Smart Support Service, using modern technology to
support care needs, as outlined in section 4 of this report at an
annual contract value of £0.806m be approved; and


2)           
the Executive Director of Adult Services, in consultation with the
Executive Director of Children and Families and the Cabinet Members
for Adult Social Care and Children and Young People, be delegated
authority to undertake all necessary actions for the implementation
of the commissioning process, including authority to award the
contract following the competitive tender exercise.
 
Reason for
Decision
 

1)           
For the Council to fulfil its statutory duty under the Care Act
2014, it should comply with the duty to provide preventative
measures to promote people’s wellbeing. In exercising this
function, the Council must have regard to the importance of
preventing or delaying the development of needs for care and
support. TEC/Smart Support is an essential service which allows
people to retain their independence and increase their autonomy,
whilst also reducing demand in other areas of care and
support.


2)           
The Council has a duty under section 17 of the Children Act 1989 to
support children in need and promote their welfare and development.
This places a general, preventative duty on local authorities to
provide services aimed at safeguarding and promoting
children’s wellbeing before compulsory intervention arises.
Smart Support will help achieve this by enhancing health,
development, communication, and family support, while reducing the
need for more intrusive interventions. It will also help children
and young people build independence as they move toward
adulthood.


3)           
This service supports the Council’s Borough Plan and the
Adult Social Care Enabling Great Lives Strategy by promoting
independence through a strength-based outcomes focused approach
that helps residents stay at home for longer. It also aligns with
the Children and Young People’s Plan 2025–2026 and the
Inclusion Matters Strategy 2023–2027 by improving the quality
and flexibility of support for children and young people, including
those with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND).
Together, these commitments ensure residents receive the support
they need at every stage of life and will continue to be carried
through into the forthcoming policy updates.


4)           
This approach is intended to support more cost-effective use of
resources over time, alongside improving outcomes for residents. In
turn, this results in cost avoidance of higher value care packages
and enables funding to be re-invested to meet growing need.
 
Alternative
Options
 

1)           
Several options were considered during the commissioning
process:
 
Option 1 – Do not
procure a new service: This would leave the Council non-compliant
with legislative requirements.
Option 2 – Procure a
new service under a whole service model: This approach provides
flexibility and innovation while ensuring continuity and stability
for operational colleagues.
Option 3 – Procure a
new service with multiple providers, in parts: Although this offers
some benefits, it presents significant risks, including
communication challenges, data sharing issues, and unnecessary
complexity.
Option 4 – Retain an
adult only service: This was discounted due to strong operational
demand for an all-age offer covering children, families, and
adults.
 

2)           
Option 2 is recommended as it delivers the greatest benefit to both
the Council and residents. It enables a flexible, innovative, and
cost-effective service capable of adapting to current and emerging
technologies.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve a new model for Smart Support to enhance independence and autonomy for residents with care needs.

content:
All local authorities in England must
develop Local SEND Reform Plans in response to the
national Schools White Paper (published 23rd Feb.
2026).  These plans focus on supporting
children and young people earlier, inclusion in mainstream schools
and improved partnership working. The plan is a local area
partnership plan, and Department for Education (DfE) guidance is
clear it must be jointly owned by the local authority and the
Integrated Care Board (ICB). The local authority is responsible for
submitting the plan to the DfE by 19th June 2026, when
it will then be reviewed and used to support discussions about
national support and funding.
 
Cheshire West and Chester has developed its
plan in partnership with the ICB and with input from the wider SEND
Partnership Board member organisations. The plan is being brought
for formal approval to enable it to be submitted by the statutory
deadline, noting it will also be approved by the SEND Partnership
Board on 15th June 2026 and the ICB Executive on
17th June 2026.

Cabinet considered the report of the Director
of Education and Inclusion which outlined the Council priorities
and plans for SEND children and young people across the Borough
with a focus on supporting them earlier, inclusion in mainstream
schools and improved partnership working. Members were informed
that a local SEND Reform Plan was a statutory requirement for all
local authorities in England, in response to the schools national
white paper entitled ‘Every Child Achieving and
Thriving’, published in February 2026.
 
Members attention was drawn to the requirement
for the plan to be a local area partnership which would be jointly
owned by the local authority and the Integrated Care Board (ICB).
This plan would be reviewed by the Department of Education (DfE)
and used to support discussions about national support and High
Needs Stability Grant funding.
 
Members noted that the principle of the reform
was to create a fully inclusive education system, increasing
inclusion with mainstream settings, that allowed children to thrive
within their local communities rather than being placed into
isolated or overly specialist environments. The reform aimed to
strengthen early intervention, enhance staff training, embed
evidence based practice, and simplify statutory processes. It would
also offer improved access to specialist advice and reduce the need
for children to travel long distances for specialist SEND support.
With increased demand for Education, Health and Care Assessment
Plans (EHCP’s), which continued to grow, the proposed SEND
reform plan outlined how additional SEND places could be made
available utilising Government capital funding.
 
Councillor Adam Langan, Cabinet Member for
Children and Young People, led the discussion on the item as
proposer and the item was seconded by Councillor Nathan Pardoe,
Cabinet Member for Inclusive Economy, Regeneration and Digital
Transformation.
 
Cabinet Members welcomed the report and
recognised the co-production and partnership of the plan between
Social Care, Health and Education services which, Members felt,
would lead to positive outcomes for inclusion. Members were
encouraged that the plan would also provide more sustainable
funding in the long-term.   
 
DECIDED:     That
 

1)           
the Local SEND Reform Plan (attached at Appendix One) be submitted
to DfE by the statutory deadline of 19 June 2026;


2)           
the Local SEND Reform Plan be taken to the SEND Partnership Board
and Integrated Care Board (ICB) Executive for their approvals prior
to submission; and


3)           
the Executive Director of Children and Families, in consultation
with the Cabinet Member for Children and Young People, be delegated
authority to make any amendments to the plan that don’t
materially change its content if required, following its approval
at SEND Partnership Board and ICB Executive, prior to submission to
the DfE.
 
Reason for
Decision
 

1)           
All local authorities in England must develop Local SEND Reform
Plans in response to the national Schools White Paper (published 23
Feb 2026).


2)           
The plan is a local area partnership plan, and DfE guidance is
clear it must be jointly owned by the local authority and the
Integrated Care Board (ICB). The local authority is responsible for
submitting the plan to the DfE by 19 June 2026 when it will then be
reviewed and used to support discussions about national support and
funding.
 
Alternative
Options
 
The Local SEND Reform Plan must be submitted
to the DfE by 19 June 2026 and must be approved by the Cabinet and
by the ICB Executive prior to submission.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the submission of the Local SEND Reform Plan to the Department for Education by the statutory deadline.

content:
Cabinet considered the report of the Executive
Director of Children and Families which sought approval to continue
participation in the Foster4 Fostering Hub collaboration and to
support the extension of the current hub model to an end-to-end
fostering model, in line with Department for Education (DfE)
expectations for future fostering reform. They further noted that
the Council wished to adopt the Gold model as part of the Foster 4
collaboration. This would support regional sufficiency, improve
recruitment and retention of foster carers and contribute to better
outcomes and stability for Children in Care.
 
Members noted that there had been a national
decline in foster carers which had led to a reliance on high cost
residential care and agencies. Despite increased payments to Foster
Carers within Cheshire West, there was still a recognised shortage.
By expanding fostering hubs to an end-to-end model, which would
cover recruitment, assessment and approval and ongoing support and
training, it was envisaged that regional coordination of
recruitment and support would see the number of foster carers
increase which would lead to more Children in Care placed in foster
homes rather than residential care.
 
Visiting Members: Councillor Charles Hardy
spoke in relation to the item.
 
Councillor Adam Langan, Cabinet Member for
Children and Young People, led the discussion on the item as
proposer and the item was seconded by Councillor Louise Gittins,
Leader of the Council. 
 
Cabinet Members welcomed the report and
recognised the positive impact that the proposals were expected to
bring, with increased foster carer recruitment and support which
would then increase the availability of appropriate foster
placements for children with a range of needs. This would allow
Children in Care to thrive through improved stability, wellbeing
and strengthening long term outcomes for Children in Care
throughout the Borough. Members were also in support of adopting
the Gold standard model which they believed would drive progress
and further improvement.
 
Members wished to thank the hard work and
dedication of all foster carers.
 
DECIDED:     That
 

1)           
Cheshire West and Chester Council continue to participate in the
Foster4 Fostering Hub, led by Warrington Borough Council, as part
of the Cheshire and Merseyside regional fostering collaboration,
with the Foster4 Hub moving towards an end-to-end fostering model
as set out in DfE guidance, subject to refreshed financial and
governance arrangements;


2)           
Cheshire West and Chester Council adopt the Gold.1 model as part of
the Foster4 collaboration (as outlined in the options paper at
appendix 1);


3)           
the contribution of further staff and/or budget to the Foster4 Hub
as Cheshire West and Chester Council’s contribution to the
end-to-end model, subject to compliance with employment law and
approval of detailed staffing and financial arrangements through
the Council’s normal governance processes, be approved in
principle; and


4)           
the Executive Director of Children and Families, in consultation
with the Director of Finance, be delegated authority to take all
necessary steps to implement the end-to-end fostering model within
the Foster4Hub arrangement.
 
Reason for
Decision
 
The Department for Education has set out a
clear expectation that all fostering hubs will move to an
end-to-end model by September 2026, with future funding contingent
on implementation. Participation in the Foster4 Hub supports
regional sufficiency, improves recruitment and retention of foster
carers, and contributes to better outcomes and stability for
children in care.
 
Alternative
Options
 
Not participating in the end-to-end Foster4
model would risk the loss of DfE funding and reduce the
Council’s ability to address foster carer sufficiency through
regional collaboration. This option is therefore not
recommended.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to continue participation in the Foster4 Fostering Hub collaboration and adopt the Gold model to improve foster carer recruitment and support.
